A privacy policy is a statement that explains in simple language how an organisation or agency handles your [personal information](https://www.oaic.gov.au/_old/privacy/your-privacy-rights/your-personal-information/what-is-personal-information).

Any organisation or agency the _[Privacy Act 1988 - external site](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Series/C2004A03712)_ covers must have a privacy policy.

A privacy policy may be printed on paper, available on a website or displayed on a mobile device’s screen. If you don’t have access to the internet, you can phone the organisation or agency and ask for a paper copy.

## What must be included
- their name and contact details
- what kinds of personal information they [collect](https://www.oaic.gov.au/_old/privacy/your-privacy-rights/your-personal-information/collection-of-personal-information) and store
- how they collect personal information and where it is stored
- the reasons why they need to collect personal information
- how they’ll [use and disclose](https://www.oaic.gov.au/_old/privacy/your-privacy-rights/your-personal-information/use-and-disclosure-of-personal-information) personal information
- how you can [access your personal information](https://www.oaic.gov.au/_old/privacy/your-privacy-rights/your-personal-information/access-your-personal-information), or [ask for a correction](https://www.oaic.gov.au/_old/privacy/your-privacy-rights/your-personal-information/correct-your-personal-information)
- how to lodge a complaint if you think your information has mishandled, and how they’ll handle your complaint
- if they are likely to disclose your information outside Australia and, if practical, which countries they are likely to disclose the information to.

If an organisation or agency’s privacy policy says that your personal information is likely to be sent overseas, if something goes wrong then they may be legally responsible.

A privacy policy may also include other information. For example, how long your personal information is kept and if it must be [scanned](https://www.oaic.gov.au/_old/privacy/your-privacy-rights/surveillance-and-monitoring/id-scanning).

## If information handling practices change
They must publicise the updated privacy policy, for example on their website and through email or postal lists.

If you can’t understand an organisation or agency’s privacy policy, ask them to explain it.

results.title: Privacy policy - Department of Home Affairs
results.description:
# Privacy policy
## 3. What personal information we collect and hold
We may collect personal information about you when it is reasonably necessary for, or directly related to, one or more of our functions or activities.

_information or an opinion about an identified individual, or an individual who is reasonably identifiable:_

- _whether the information or opinion is true or not; and_
- _whether the information or opinion is recorded in a material form or not._

We may also collect sensitive information about you:

- where you consent
- when the collection is authorised or required by law
- where the collection is otherwise allowed under the Privacy Act.

- information or an opinion about an individual’s:
  - racial or ethnic origin
  - political opinions
  - membership of a political association
  - religious beliefs or affiliations
  - philosophical beliefs
  - membership of a professional or trade association
  - membership of a trade union
  - sexual orientation or practices
  - criminal record

that is also personal information

## 4. How we collect your personal information
Our usual practice is to collect personal information directly from the individual or their authorised representative.

Your personal information may also be collected and managed via our ImmiAccount and Visa Entitlement Verification Online (VEVO) platforms.

We often also collect personal information from other sources. These include third parties or publicly available sources.

- federal, state, and territory government and law enforcement agencies
- medical practitioners
- employers
- members of the public who contact us with information
- third party carriers, such as commercial airlines and cruise operators
- open-source tools, including with the assistance of software
- social media.

## Visits to our website
- discover what information is most and least accessed
- make the website more useful.

## Quality of personal information
- inaccurate
- out-of-date
- incomplete
- irrelevant
- misleading.

results.title: Privacy policy - Wikipedia
results.description:
For Wikipedia's privacy policy, see [Wikimedia Foundation Privacy Policy](https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Privacy_policy). A **privacy policy** is a statement or legal document (in privacy law) that discloses some or all of the ways a party gathers, uses, discloses, and manages a customer or client's [data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_data),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy_policy#cite_note-1) while a **privacy notice** tells clients or data subjects what data is held by an organisation and how that data will be handled. Personal information can be anything that can be used to identify an individual, not limited to the person's name, address, date of birth, marital status, contact information, ID issue, and expiry date, financial records, credit information, medical history, where one travels, and intentions to acquire goods and services. [[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy_policy#cite_note-3) In the case of a business, it is often a statement that declares a party's policy on how it collects, stores, and releases personal information it collects. [[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy_policy#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy_policy#cite_note-5) Privacy policies typically represent a broader, more generalized treatment, as opposed to data use statements, which tend to be more detailed and specific. The exact contents of a privacy policy will depend upon the applicable law and may need to address requirements across geographical boundaries and legal jurisdictions. Their privacy laws apply not only to government operations but also to private enterprises and commercial transactions. ## History All this led the council to recommend that policy be developed to protect [personal data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_data) held by both the private and public sectors, leading to Convention 108. In the United States, concern over privacy policy starting around the late 1960s and 1970s led to the passage of the [Fair Credit Reporting Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Credit_Reporting_Act). ## Applicable law ### India The privacy policy should be published on the website of the body corporate, and be made available for view by providers of information who have provided personal information under lawful contract. ## Criticism [[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy_policy#cite_note-54) However, the same study also showed that when information about privacy practices is clearly presented, consumers prefer retailers who better protect their privacy and some are willing to "pay a premium to purchase from more privacy protective websites". [[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy_policy#cite_note-55) Based on the common nature of this misunderstanding, researcher Joseph Turow argued to the U.S. [Federal Trade Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Trade_Commission) that the term "privacy policy" thus constitutes a deceptive trade practice and that alternative phrasing like "how we use your information" should be used instead. Privacy policies suffer generally from a lack of precision, especially when compared with the emerging form of the Data Use Statement. [[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy_policy#cite_note-60) However, any efforts to make the information more presentable simplify the information to the point that it does not convey the extent to which users' data is being shared and sold. ## Further reading | hide
